newsitem.title: GERMANY: Weak Europe, rivals dampen Intel demand.
newsitem.headline: Weak Europe, rivals dampen Intel demand.

text.p: Intel Corp is feeling pressure in Europe because of economic uncertainty in the region as well as gains by rival microchip makers, computer industry analysts said on Monday.

Stagnant economies, austerity measures related to European monetary union and transitions to new Intel chips were dampening demand for personal computers, especially among consumers, the analysts said.
At the same time, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Cyrix Corp. were winning sales from some notable PC makers, they said.

"The (European) market is showing single-digit growth rates, and that will continue," said Philip Williams at International Data Corp. in London. "The slow-down is caused by pressure on countries to make monetary union, and that's hitting individuals and firms alike."

Intel shares on Friday tumbled more than $12 to $151.50 after the company said weak demand, especially in Europe, would cause second-quarter sales to come in five to 10 percent below the first-quarter total of $6.4 billion.
Some analysts said introductions of Pentium chips with MMX multimedia technology in January weakened sales of older Pentium chips earlier this year.
"There were more (older Pentium chips) left in the channel at the end of the first than we would normally expect," said Dataquest's Joe D'Elia in Egham, England.
D'Elia said he expected Intel's demand situation to improve after PC makers sell off machiens made from Pentium chips that don't have multimedia capabilities.
"I expect this to be a temporary factor," he said.
An Intel spokesman in Munich said on Monday the company was at a loss to explain the drop in European demand.
"We don't know why (demand is weak), either," Intel spokesman Heiner Genzken told Reuters. "We see no signs (competitors) are winning market share."
But AMD and Cyrix, which have finally released chips that can match Intel products in performance, were making inroads, the analysts said.

"They have come out with some very strong products and it seems they are in for more market share," said Emmanuel Lalloz at market researcher Context. "Intel doesn't have complete control of the industry."
Fujitsu, which has a 3.7 percent market share in Europe, and Vobis Microcomputer AG, one of Germany's largest PC makers, have agreed to use AMD's K6 processor.
Meanwhile, Compaq Computer Corp. in the first quarter introduced a home PC with a Cyrix chip. IBM Corp. manufactures chips for Cyrix and uses some in its PCs.
Compaq and IBM continue to use Intel chips for their most expensive and powerful machines. Others like Dell Computer Corp. plan to use only Intel chip.
Genzken, the Intel spokesman, said demand was strong for Intel's fastest chips -- the Pentium II and Pentium with MMX multimedia capabilities. "Demand is greater than we can deliver," he said.
But demand for standard Pentium chips was "very weak," he said. Intel does not break out its sales mix by products, Genzken said. He also declined to say what countries were showing weakest demand.
